newsitem.title: CHINA: China law to expand highways, affirm foreign role.
newsitem.headline: China law to expand highways, affirm foreign role.

text.p: China said on Friday it had approved a law to spur the expansion of badly needed highways by putting its stamp of approval on foreign investment and the sale of stocks and bonds to raise funds.

The nation's first comprehensive highway law, approved by parliament last week, was aimed at encouraging road construction and clarifying management -- including the sensitive issue of collecting tolls.
"This law is a milestone in the construction of our communications network," Vice Minister of Communications Li Juchang told reporters.
"Companies that develop or operate highways can raise funds by issuing stock and corporate bonds according to law and administrative regulations," he said.
Under the law, which takes effect on January 1 next year, authorities have the right to set tolls to recoup investment and pay for maintenance.
Chinese officials said they needed $60 billion dollars for highway construction during the 1995-2000 period and they wanted 10 percent to be raised from foreign investment and loans.

They estimated that China's own funds were 10-25 percent short of the total needed to build another 92,000 km (57,000 miles) of roads -- including at least 8,000 km (5,000 miles) of major highways -- during the nation's current five-year plan.
"Our shortage of funds for road construction is considerable," said Li.
China has already taken rapid strides in allowing foreign investors to build and operate highways and has allowed highway management companies to sell shares to foreign investors.
Even without the comprehensive law, numerous foreign companies have been courted to help fill the financial gap in the plans for road construction.
Officials said the law also was aimed at halting the unauthorised collection of tolls.
"We need controls over the arbitrary setting up of toll booths," said Wu Fuzhao, senior economist and a parliament member who helped draft the law.
He said that as roads straddle county and provincial lines, local governments had set up too many toll collection points and this problem was addressed in the highway law.
"We have to impose some kind of control on the arbitrary collection of tolls," he said.
The law also seeks to define responsibility for road management both at the central government level as well as for local government levels.
It also requires that funds raised from toll collection must go to road maintenance and not be diverted to other uses.
Officials also said the law did not change the application procedure for foreign companies seeking to take part in the construction or management of roads.
